p: Slavery is as old as civilisation. It existed in Mesopotamia and Egypt, in Greece and Rome, in China and India, in Africa and the Americas, in the Islamic world and in medieval Christendom. Aristotle held that some men are slaves by nature, and the laws of Hammurabi, of Moses and of Justinian all regulate it. I say this not to excuse what follows, but to make clear what was new in it. The Atlantic slave trade, which carried Africans to the Americas from the early sixteenth century to the middle of my own, was not new in kind. It was new in its scale, in its distances, in its organisation as a great commercial enterprise, and in its foundation upon the colour of the skin.

The Portuguese began it, buying slaves on the coast of West Africa in the fifteenth century for their sugar plantations on the Atlantic islands. When sugar came to Brazil and the Caribbean, and the native peoples died in their multitudes, the planters turned to Africa. The first ship to carry slaves directly from Africa to the Americas sailed, the Encyclopaedia records, in fifteen twenty-six. Over the following three and a half centuries, some twelve and a half million Africans were embarked on the ships of the trade, of whom something under eleven million arrived alive. These figures come from a great list of slave voyages compiled by the scholars of the future, who have gathered the records of more than thirty-six thousand of them. Nearly half went to Brazil. Most of the rest went to the sugar islands of the Caribbean, British, French, Spanish and Dutch. A much smaller number, perhaps four hundred thousand, went to the mainland of North America, where, unlike in the Caribbean, their numbers grew by natural increase.

Every nation of Western Europe with a coast took part, and the British, in the eighteenth century, more than any other. Bristol, Liverpool and London grew rich upon it. The trade was often described as a triangle: ships carried cloth, guns, brandy and metal goods from Europe to Africa; exchanged them for captives; carried the captives across the Atlantic, on what was called the Middle Passage; and returned with sugar, tobacco, cotton and rum, the products of slave labour.

The captives were mostly sold to European traders by African rulers and merchants, who obtained them by war, by raiding, by judicial punishment and by kidnapping. The trade could not have existed without African partners, and it corrupted and devastated great regions of Africa, drawing whole kingdoms into the business of manhunting. But the demand that drove it came from the Americas, and the ships, the capital and the profits were European.

The voyage across the Atlantic took from five weeks to three months. The captives were chained and packed below decks in spaces where they could not sit upright, in heat, darkness and filth. Disease, especially dysentery, killed many; some refused food and were forced to eat; some threw themselves into the sea. The Encyclopaedia estimates that on average perhaps one in eight died on the voyage, and many more in the march to the coast before it and the first months after. A plan of the Liverpool ship Brookes, published by the abolitionists in seventeen eighty-eight, showed the captives laid out in rows like books upon a shelf. It was one of the most effective pieces of propaganda ever made, and its effect came from its accuracy.

On the plantations, especially the sugar estates, the labour was so severe and the treatment so harsh that in many colonies the enslaved died faster than they were born, and were replaced by fresh purchases from Africa. The planters calculated, quite coldly, that it was cheaper to work a man to death and buy another than to keep him in health.

That such a system, so profitable and so long established, should have been overthrown is one of the great moral events in history, and I count myself fortunate to have lived through its later stages. Opposition came first from the Quakers, in America and England, who held that every human being contains the light of God. In seventeen eighty-seven, a committee was formed in London, led by Thomas Clarkson, who gathered evidence with tireless courage in the ports, and Granville Sharp, and with William Wilberforce, the member of Parliament for Yorkshire, as its voice in the House of Commons. Former slaves, above all Olaudah Equiano, whose autobiography of seventeen eighty-nine described his capture as a boy and his life in slavery, told their own stories. Josiah Wedgwood, the potter, made a medallion showing a kneeling African in chains with the words: am I not a man and a brother? Hundreds of thousands of English people refused to eat sugar grown by slaves, and petitions with enormous numbers of signatures were sent to Parliament.

The enslaved also freed themselves. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the richest in the world, the slaves rose in seventeen ninety-one, and under the leadership of a former slave of genius, Toussaint Louverture, defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain, and founded in eighteen hundred and four the free republic of Haiti. In the British Caribbean, great rebellions, in Jamaica in eighteen thirty-one above all, convinced many in Parliament that slavery could not be maintained.

Britain abolished the trade in eighteen hundred and seven, and slavery itself in its colonies by an act of eighteen thirty-three, which came into force the following year; I remember the bells. The government paid twenty million pounds in compensation, not to the enslaved, but to their owners, a sum that the men of the future reckon at some forty per cent of the government's annual spending. The navy was sent to suppress the trade on the African coast. The United States ended slavery only after a civil war in which six hundred thousand men died, ten years ago, and Brazil, the Encyclopaedia tells me, will be the last nation in the Americas to abolish it, in eighteen eighty-eight.

Abolition did not end the suffering. The freed peoples of the Caribbean and America were left landless and poor, and in the American South the Encyclopaedia records a century of legal segregation, violence and disenfranchisement before the movement for civil rights of the nineteen-fifties and sixties. The idea, invented to justify the trade, that Africans were by nature inferior, outlived the trade by many generations. And Africa itself, in the years to come, was to be divided among the European powers, often in the name of suppressing the slave trade that Europe had created. I record these things as a historian must. I would add, as an old man, that the abolitionists proved something worth remembering: that a great evil, sanctioned by law, custom and profit, can be overthrown by people who refuse to stop talking about it.
